source.title: How does unlabeled data improve generalization in self-training? A one-hidden-layer theoretical analysis
source.authors: Shuai Zhang; M. Wang; Si-Jia Liu; Pin-Yu Chen; Jin-Jun Xiong

record.tranche_reason: The paper reports its own self-training experiments, including deep networks on augmented CIFAR-10, but studies generalization and convergence in a semi-supervised setting rather than the claim’s training classification error on CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100.
record.gate_note: Rows below cover reported outcomes for self-training on augmented CIFAR-10 and synthetic-data experiments bearing on CIFAR-10 or deep-network behavior. The paper does not report CIFAR-100, corrupted or random labels, or training classification error as described by V1. Theoretical statements and cited prior-work results are not rows.
record.test_reason: The study measures self-training generalization, weight recovery and convergence as unlabeled data change. It does not test any specified version: CIFAR-10 results concern test accuracy, teacher-student experiments fix width and start near ground truth, and there are no relevant initialization, depth, learning-rate stability or normalization comparisons.
record.authors_conclusion: The record is broadly correct but needs qualification: under Gaussian one-hidden-layer assumptions, nearby initialization and suitable sample sizes and loss weights, the authors prove linear convergence with bounds containing terms of order 1/√M. Zero generalization error and a constant-factor reduction in labeled-sample requirements require the stronger conditions of Theorem 2. Synthetic and CIFAR-10 experiments illustrate the predicted trends.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes iterative semi-supervised self-training, including pseudo-labeling, rather than the claim’s random-initialization gradient-training recipes for training classification error. The theoretical model is a one-hidden-layer ReLU regression network with Gaussian inputs; the image experiment uses augmented CIFAR-10 and a cited implementation.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that convergence worsens when unlabeled-data variance δ̃ increases above 1; relative error first decreases with λ̂ and then increases beyond a threshold correlated with N.

fits_no_version.finding: Self-training improves CIFAR-10 test accuracy by up to 7% using unlabeled data; exact condition-specific accuracies cannot be recovered from the supplied plot text.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Additional unlabeled data can improve test accuracy under the studied iterative self-training recipe.

fits_no_version.finding: At fixed width 10 and initialization near ground truth, additional unlabeled data improve weight recovery and convergence and reduce labeled-sample requirements; distribution scale and loss weighting affect these benefits.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Iterative self-training can improve local weight recovery and convergence under the studied Gaussian teacher-student conditions.

fits_no_version.finding: Figure 11 reports CIFAR-10 convergence factors calculated over the first 50 epochs, approximately linear in 1/√M, for N = 15K, 30K and 50K.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Unlabeled-data quantity affects early convergence under the studied CIFAR-10 self-training recipe.

record.problems: The theory assumes Gaussian inputs and a nearby initialization; experiments use a one-hidden-layer synthetic model and a single augmented CIFAR-10 setting. The CIFAR-10 test-accuracy values are shown only in a figure, with no explicit baseline value in the text. Training classification error is not reported.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant reported outcomes were omitted. The paper's theoretical convergence and error bounds are not empirical result rows; cited prior-work results are excluded.

untested.parts: All parts: training classification error, random initialization, CIFAR-100, corrupted labels, and size or training-recipe comparisons.
All parts: spurious-minimum frequencies from standard initialization, jointly increasing teacher/student widths, and extra student neurons.
All parts: training-error degradation with depth and prevention through shortcuts or the specified alternative recipes.
All parts: activation-matched initialization, signal and gradient preservation, orthogonal/Gaussian comparisons, and trainable depth.
All parts: learning-rate stability thresholds, transient loss increases, curvature dynamics and divergence.
All parts: normalization comparisons for training speed and learning-rate tolerance, including Fixup.

record.verdict_notes: States describe whether rows establish a specified version, so unrelated rows receive cannot_determine even when their own reported trends are clear. Figure 4's depth-dependent relationship between weight distance and population error does not measure depth-dependent training failure. Tensor initialization is a prerequisite here, not a test of V4. Citations to Safran and Shamir and batch normalization provide background, not new tests.

versions.untested_parts: Training classification error from random initialization; CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100 supervised or corrupted-label training; model size, early stopping, and regularization conditions.
Teacher-student spurious minima and the effect of extra student neurons.
Depth effects on training error with and without identity shortcuts, plain tanh networks, and residual networks without normalization.
Activation-matched initialization, orthogonal versus Gaussian initialization, and training depth.
Learning-rate stability thresholds, curvature, loss increases, and divergence.
Batch normalization's effect on training speed and learning-rate tolerance, and Fixup comparisons.

rows.subject: self-training on augmented CIFAR-10 dataset
rows.operation_detail: Iterative self-training using the implementation from Carmon et al. (2019), with unlabeled images mined from 80 Million Tiny Images.
rows.note: The text says test accuracy improves using unlabeled data, but does not state the plotted value at zero unlabeled data. This is a generalization outcome, not training classification error.
rows.check: Test accuracy cannot establish V1's training classification error; the exact plotted accuracy is unavailable.

rows.subject: self-training on synthetic data
rows.operation_detail: Iterative self-training; relative error averaged over 1000 independent trials.
rows.measure: relative error decreases as unlabeled data or labeled data increases
rows.value: explicitly stated trend; plotted values figure only
rows.note: This reports weight-relative error and theoretical generalization behavior, not training classification error.
rows.check: The reported weight-recovery trend is explicit, but measures none of V1–V6. Width is fixed at 10 and initialization is within relative distance 0.5 of ground truth.

rows.subject: self-training on synthetic data
rows.operation_detail: Iterative self-training; convergence-rate results averaged over 1000 independent trials.
rows.measure: convergence rate improves as unlabeled data increases and is linear in 1/√M
rows.value: explicitly stated trend; plotted values figure only
rows.note: A convergence-rate measure, not training classification error.
rows.check: Unlabeled-data effects on convergence measure none of V1–V6. Figure 6 includes N = 250, 300 and 350; the row's N = 250 condition captures only one curve.

rows.subject: self-training on synthetic data
rows.operation_detail: Iterative self-training; convergence-rate results averaged over 1000 independent trials.
rows.value: convergence becomes worse as δ̃ increases from 1; for δ̃ less than 1 it almost remains the same
rows.note: A convergence-rate measure, not training classification error.
rows.check: Changing the unlabeled input distribution measures none of V1–V6. δ̃ is the Gaussian standard-deviation parameter; its variance is δ̃², despite the paper's loose terminology.

rows.subject: self-training on synthetic data
rows.operation_detail: Iterative self-training; relative errors averaged over 1000 independent trials.
rows.measure: relative error of returned weights to ground-truth weights
rows.value: error decreases almost linearly as λ̂ increases, then increases when λ exceeds a threshold positively correlated with N
rows.note: The authors state the higher-λ̂ trend has an upper limit that increases with N; this is a generalization-related weight error, not classification error.
rows.check: Changing the labeled-data weight measures none of V1–V6. λ̂ is a loss-mixture parameter, not a learning rate; its threshold does not test V5.

rows.subject: self-training on synthetic data
rows.operation_detail: Phase-transition experiment; 100 independent trials for every pair of d and N.
rows.measure: successful trials for learning ground-truth weights
rows.value: white blocks indicate successful trials; black block indicates all failures; exact counts figure only
rows.note: The text says the required labeled sample complexity is linear in d; no training classification error is measured.
rows.check: Success means relative weight error ≤ 0.01, not zero training classification error or avoidance of spurious minima from standard initialization.

rows.subject: self-training on synthetic data
rows.operation_detail: Phase-transition experiment; 100 independent trials for every pair of d and N.
rows.measure: successful trials for learning ground-truth weights
rows.value: phase-transition line is below the one when M = 0; exact counts figure only
rows.note: The paper states unlabeled data reduce the required sample complexity of N; no training classification error is measured.
